parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State what is meant by nuclear fusion.
hints: Hint 1: Think about the word fusion itself - it means joining or merging. What objects are involved in a nuclear reaction?
Hint 2: For full credit you need to say how many nuclei start the process and what single product is formed. Contrast with fission which splits.
parts.proper_answer: Nuclear fusion is the joining together of two small light nuclei to form one larger heavier nucleus.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture What Happens to the Nuclei**
Imagine two very light nuclei, like hydrogen isotopes, forced so close together that the strong nuclear force grabs them. Fusion is the opposite of fission. Instead of splitting apart, things come together.

Step 2: **State the Definition Clearly**
You need both ideas for two marks: two small nuclei join together, and they form a single larger nucleus. Energy is released in the process because the product is more tightly bound, but the definition itself is just about joining to make one heavier nucleus.

hints: Hint 1: Recall where the most stable nucleus sits on the A axis and what the value at A = 1 must be.
Hint 2: Think about how fast the curve rises for light nuclei compared to how it falls for heavy nuclei, and whether it ever reaches zero again.
parts.proper_answer: Curve starting near zero at A = 1, rising steeply to a peak at A approx 56, then falling slowly with shallow negative gradient to A = 250, remaining well above zero.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Remember the Famous Shape**
Binding energy per nucleon tells you how stable a nucleus is. It starts very low for hydrogen and helium, climbs very steeply as small nuclei add nucleons, reaches a maximum around iron with $A \approx 56$, then gently slopes down for heavier nuclei.

Step 2: **Sketch It Accurately**
Start your line just above zero at $A = 1$. Draw a steep rise up to the peak at $A \approx 56$. Then draw a long, shallow fall to $A = 250$. The right-hand end must stay high, around 7-8 MeV, never dropping back to zero.

hints: Hint 1: Alpha decay happens to very heavy, less stable nuclei that can become more stable by losing mass - which side of the peak are they on?
parts.proper_answer: Point X marked on the curve at high A, well to the right of the peak (e.g. A > 150).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Alpha Decay to Heavy Nuclei**
Alpha decay ejects a helium-4 nucleus and reduces $A$ by 4. Only very heavy nuclei to the right of the peak do this, moving leftwards up the curve to higher binding energy per nucleon and greater stability. So place X far to the right on your falling section.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text:
A nucleus $Z$ undergoes nuclear fission to form strontium-93 ($^{93}_{38}\text{Sr}$) and xenon-139 ($^{139}_{54}\text{Xe}$) according to

$${}^{1}_{0}\text{n} + Z \rightarrow {}^{93}_{38}\text{Sr} + {}^{139}_{54}\text{Xe} + 2{}^{1}_{0}\text{n}.$$

Table 9.1 shows the binding energies of the strontium-93 and xenon-139 nuclei.

Table 9.1

nucleus | binding energy / $\text{J}$
$^{93}_{38}\text{Sr}$ | $1.25 \times 10^{-10}$
$^{139}_{54}\text{Xe}$ | $1.81 \times 10^{-10}$

The fission of $1.00\text{ mol}$ of $Z$ releases $1.77 \times 10^{13}\text{ J}$ of energy.

Determine the binding energy per nucleon, in $\text{MeV}$, of $Z$.
hints: Hint 1: The given energy is for one mole. How do you get the energy released in a single fission event?

Hint 2: Fission products are more tightly bound than the parent, and the difference appears as released energy. How can you use the two product binding energies and the released energy to find the parent binding energy?
Hint 3: Use nucleon number balance on the equation to find how many nucleons are in nucleus Z.
Hint 4: To finish, divide by nucleon number and convert the small joule value to MeV using $1 \text{ eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$.
parts.proper_answer: Energy per fission $= 2.94 \times 10^{-11} \text{ J}$, binding energy of Z $= 2.77 \times 10^{-10} \text{ J}$, $A_Z = 233$, binding energy per nucleon $= 7.43 \text{ MeV}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find Energy Released Per Nucleus**
One mole contains $N_A = 6.02 \times 10^{23}$ nuclei. So divide the molar energy by $N_A$:
$$E_{1} = \frac{1.77 \times 10^{13}}{6.02 \times 10^{23}} \approx 2.94 \times 10^{-11} \text{ J}$$
This is the extra binding that appears as kinetic energy and gamma rays.

Step 2: **Use Binding Energy Balance to Find BE of Z**
Binding energy increases in fission:
$$E_{released} = BE_{products} - BE_{Z}$$
$$BE_{products} = 1.25 \times 10^{-10} + 1.81 \times 10^{-10} = 3.06 \times 10^{-10} \text{ J}$$
Rearrange:
$$BE_{Z} = BE_{products} - E_{1}$$
$$BE_{Z} = 3.06 \times 10^{-10} - 2.94 \times 10^{-11} \approx 2.77 \times 10^{-10} \text{ J}$$

Step 3: **Find Nucleon Number of Z**
Nucleons are conserved. Count top numbers:
$$1 + A_Z = 93 + 139 + 2$$
$$A_Z = 93 + 139 + 2 - 1 = 233$$

Step 4: **Divide and Convert to MeV**
Binding energy per nucleon in joules:
$$\frac{BE_Z}{A_Z} = \frac{2.77 \times 10^{-10}}{233} \approx 1.19 \times 10^{-12} \text{ J}$$
Since $1 \text{ MeV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-13} \text{ J}$:
$$BE \text{ per nucleon} = \frac{1.19 \times 10^{-12}}{1.60 \times 10^{-13}} \approx 7.43 \text{ MeV}$$
